extracted.intended_audience: workers, employers, unions, safety professionals, small businesses, and other stakeholders who want to participate in OSHA rulemaking
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for members of the public on how to engage in OSHA's rulemaking process and how to prepare and submit effective comments, testimony, and data at each rulemaking stage. Covers procedural steps (RFIs/ANPRMs/NPRMs/SBREFA/hearings), submission methods, and content suggestions for comments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make clear your position and explain impacts
rubrics_metrics.description: The most helpful comments clearly communicate whether you are for or against the proposed action, why, and how it impacts you.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: State your position (support/oppose), give reasons, and describe how the proposal affects you personally, other workers, or your industry. Be explicit about impacts so OSHA can understand the practical consequences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plan ahead and meet the comment deadline
rubrics_metrics.description: Plan Ahead. The comment period closes at 11:59 p.m. Eastern Time on the date comments are due.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Know the deadline published in the Federal Register for each RFI/ANPRM/NPRM and submit before that time. Late comments may not be considered.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contact OSHA with questions before commenting
rubrics_metrics.description: Contact OSHA. If you have questions or do not understand a part of the document, reach out to the contact person listed on the Federal Register before submitting your comment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the point of contact listed in the Federal Register notice to clarify scope, definitions, or procedural questions so your comment can be targeted and relevant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tell your story with specific examples and details
rubrics_metrics.description: Tell us your story. In your comment, tell us how the issue impacts you, other workers, or your industry. Provide as much detail as possible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include concrete descriptions of workplace hazards, incidents, exposures, dates, job tasks, numbers affected, and any outcomes (injury, illness). Specific, concrete anecdotes are especially helpful, and workers' perspectives are emphasized.

rubrics_metrics.name: Explain what has worked and propose concrete solutions
rubrics_metrics.description: What has worked to make your workplace safer? What can OSHA do to make your workplace safer?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Describe existing controls, practices, or interventions that reduced hazards and offer practical, implementable suggestions or alternatives for OSHA to consider. Be specific about feasibility and expected benefits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Answer agency questions and provide supporting data
rubrics_metrics.description: Each RFI, ANPRM, and NPRM announces a comment period when the public can submit written comments, data, and answers to questions posed by the agency.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Respond directly to the questions the notice asks. Include empirical data, studies, measurements, or other documentation that support your assertions. Attach or reference evidence where possible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tailor comments to the rulemaking stage and document type
rubrics_metrics.description: RFIs are generally used when OSHA is determining whether to proceed with regulation and, if so, what general approach to take. ANPRMs are generally used when the agency has developed multiple regulatory options and seeks input on which option to propose.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For pre-rule RFIs focus on whether regulation is needed and on possible general approaches; for ANPRMs compare and evaluate proposed options; for NPRMs comment on the proposed rule text, basis, and analyses. Tailor content to the document's purpose and the stage of rulemaking.

rubrics_metrics.name: You do not have to comment on everything; identify agreement and disagreement
rubrics_metrics.description: Remember, you do not have to comment on every question or section of the document. If there are parts where you agree and other sections where you disagree, please let us know.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be selective if helpful: specify which provisions you support and which you oppose, and explain why. Clarify which aspects matter most to you and prioritize those in your comment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use the authorized submission methods listed in the notice
rubrics_metrics.description: You can submit comments: Online at Regulations.gov, By mail, or In person at certain locations. The rule published in the Federal Register will provide details on where to send comments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow the submission instructions in the Federal Register notice (including submission format, docket number, and any filing requirements). If submitting electronically, use Regulations.gov and follow attachment/format rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Small businesses should use SBREFA to explain economic impacts
rubrics_metrics.description: The SBREFA process allows small business employers to let OSHA know how the proposed rule will affect their businesses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Small business representatives should participate in SBREFA panels or provide comments that explain compliance costs, economic burdens, or feasibility concerns; include specific cost estimates or operational constraints where possible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Follow procedures to testify at public meetings or hearings
rubrics_metrics.description: The public may be asked to speak at meetings such as those of federal advisory committees, stakeholder meetings, or send in written comments. If OSHA holds a public hearing, the schedule for the hearing is published in the Federal Register, with detailed information on how to participate, including instructions for submitting Notices of Intention to appear (NOITA).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If you intend to speak at a hearing, submit a NOITA as instructed, prepare oral testimony that complements written comments, and be ready to answer questions. Check the Federal Register for hearing logistics and any time limits or format rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider confidentiality and retaliation concerns when describing worker health information
rubrics_metrics.description: Workers expressed fear of retaliation or discrimination if employers knew they had an illness; OSHA addressed this by limiting types of information healthcare providers could provide without worker permission in a past rule.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If your comment involves sensitive health or personnel information, explain confidentiality concerns and, if relevant, request protections or redactions. Describe fears of retaliation and, where possible, suggest safeguards to protect workers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Monitor rule status and use OSHA/Regulations.gov resources
rubrics_metrics.description: Learn What OSHA Is up to: Subscribe to QuickTakes; View rules Open for Public Comments; and Visit Frequently Asked Questions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Stay informed about open dockets, outreach events, and instructional resources (videos, FAQs). Use these channels to learn how to comment, track deadlines, and find supporting materials.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide evidence and reasoning because OSHA will analyze comments and respond
rubrics_metrics.description: OSHA analyzes the rulemaking record leading to the rule, including all public comments and other information the agency has collected to develop the final rule, which presents an explanation of the rule's requirements including OSHA's analysis that support its decisions and OSHA's responses to the public comments on the NPRM.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Submit comments that include factual evidence, logical argumentation, and citations so OSHA can incorporate or respond to them in the final rule. Anticipate the agency's need to document its reasoning and supply materials that can be referenced in the administrative record.
